design_rules: Wall thickness and aspect ratio: target t ≥ 1.5–2.0 mm for side walls (absolute minimum ~1.0 mm if very short); wall height/thickness ≤10:1 during roughing and ≤15:1 after finishing; pocket floors ≥1.0–1.5 mm.

Internal radii and tool access: avoid sharp inside corners; use internal corner radii ≥ tool radius + 0.5 mm (practical minimum ~1.0 mm). Prefer generous fillets; add external fillets to reduce chatter and stress.
Pocket/slot depth vs tool diameter: limit effective cutting depth to ≤3× tool diameter; design for the largest possible tool; make pockets open-ended or add reliefs for tool entry/exit.
Uniform sections: keep wall thickness as uniform as possible; balance material removal across the part to minimize distortion; avoid isolated thin ‘islands’.

Stiffening features: add ribs/webs to support thin walls (rib thickness ~0.6–1.0× adjacent wall, spaced 20–40 mm); use bosses or thicker pads around holes; avoid threading directly into thin walls—use inserts or increased thickness.
Feature edge distances: keep hole/slot edge distance ≥2× diameter (absolute minimum ~1.5×); maintain spacing between adjacent holes ≥1× diameter.

Tolerances and finish: tighten only where functional; expect flatness/parallelism to degrade with size and thinness; economical Ra ≈ 1.6–3.2 µm; specify break-edges/chamfers and allowable burr condition.

Manufacturing allowances: design fixturing tabs or sacrificial stock; provide consistent datums; allow 0.2–0.5 mm finish stock on thin features; include lead-in/out reliefs for entry without wall push-off.
Tool reach and deflection: avoid deep, narrow features requiring >8–10× diameter stick-out; provide side access; consider 5-axis accessibility to reduce long-reach tools and improve stability.

Distortion control: choose stable, stress-relieved plate and suitable temper (e.g., 6061‑T6, 7075‑T6); plan intermediate stress relief for heavy stock removal; use light finishing passes and controlled coolant to limit thermal distortion.

answer_json.summary: Thin-walled aluminum parts are prone to chatter, deflection, and distortion. Favor uniform, adequately thick walls (≥1.5–2.0 mm) with controlled aspect ratios, generous internal radii, and shallow pockets sized for large, stiff tools. Add ribs, bosses, and thicker pads where loads or threads occur, and keep holes away from edges (≥2× diameter). Apply tight tolerances and fine finishes only where necessary; expect flatness to worsen as parts get thinner and larger. Enable stable machining with consistent datums, sacrificial stock/tabs, reliefs for tool entry, and 0.2–0.5 mm finish stock for light, stable finishing passes. Minimize long tool reach (≤8–10× diameter) or provide 5-axis access. Use stress-relieved plate and suitable tempers, consider stress relief between roughing and finishing, and use light finishing to control distortion. Share alloy, tolerances, size, finish, and machine constraints to refine these rules.

design_rules: Default to climb milling on modern CNC/ball-screw machines with minimal backlash; it yields better surface finish, dimensional accuracy, and lower cutting forces due to thick-to-thin chip formation.
Use conventional milling on manual/older machines or any setup with noticeable backlash to prevent the cutter from pulling the table/work into the cut.
Prioritize conventional milling for the first roughing pass on cast skin, flame-cut edges, scale, or abrasive surfaces; finish with climb to improve accuracy and finish.
For work-hardening or gummy materials (e.g., stainless, nickel alloys, aluminum), prefer climb to minimize rubbing and work-hardening; ensure rigid fixturing.
For abrasive/brittle materials (e.g., cast iron or composites), consider conventional for roughing to protect the cutting edge; climb for finishing if the setup is rigid.
On thin walls or flexible parts, use light radial engagement climb passes to reduce burrs and deflection; if pull-in risk exists, switch to conventional or improve fixturing.
During full-width slotting, rough conventionally to avoid grabbing, then offset and finish each wall with a light climb pass.
Carbide tools generally benefit from climb milling; HSS tools on less rigid machines may fare better with conventional to avoid edge chipping from pull-in.
If chatter or poor finish appears in climb due to insufficient rigidity, reduce radial engagement, increase feed per tooth slightly, or switch to conventional for stability.
Plan burr location: climb tends to form burrs at entry, conventional at exit; choose direction to move burrs to a non-critical edge.

answer_json.summary: Choose climb milling on rigid, low-backlash CNC setups—especially for finishing, aluminum, and work-hardening alloys—because the chip goes thick-to-thin, reducing rubbing, improving finish, and lowering tool wear. Use conventional milling when backlash or poor rigidity risks the cutter pulling the work, and for the first pass on scale, cast skin, or abrasive edges. For slotting, rough conventionally, then finish walls with light climb passes. Thin or flexible parts benefit from light radial climb if well-fixtured; otherwise switch to conventional. Carbide favors climb; HSS on less rigid machines may prefer conventional. Manage burr location by choosing direction: climb burrs at entry, conventional at exit. If climb chatters, decrease radial engagement, ensure proper feed per tooth, or revert to conventional. Provide machine type/backlash, material/condition, fixturing rigidity, tool details, and cut parameters to finalize the recommendation.
